projects.title: Live Status Dashboard
projects.description: Real-time health checks, uptime, and an outage log. React, TypeScript, Jest.

caseStudy.problem: Health check results only help if someone notices a problem the moment it starts. My aws-healthcheck-iac project writes health checks to a JSON report, so I built a dashboard that shows that report live and makes outages obvious.
built: Summary cards and trend lines for pass rate and latency, refreshed every 5 seconds
Uptime for each check and a strip of recent results, so a flapping check stands out
A log of every outage and recovery with the time and the error
Search, a status filter, and sortable columns
CSV export that neutralizes spreadsheet formula injection
If a refresh fails, an error banner appears and the last good data stays on screen
results: 87 Jest and React Testing Library tests
No WCAG 2.1 AA issues found by axe-core in light and dark mode
A live demo on GitHub Pages, deployed automatically, with all data synthetic

projects.title: CSV Quality Gate
projects.description: Checks CSV files against rules, quarantines bad rows, and fails CI on bad data.

caseStudy.problem: Bad rows in a CSV file, like missing values, typos, and duplicates, quietly break reports and imports. Teams need a check that stops bad data before it is loaded.
built: A JSON rules file for types, ranges, allowed values, patterns, uniqueness, date ranges, and blank limits
Rules that compare two columns, like ship date on or after order date
infer, which drafts a rules file from a known-good CSV
Quarantine that splits rows into passed and failed files with the reasons
JSON, Markdown, HTML, and JUnit reports, and a reusable GitHub Action
results: 129 tests, including Hypothesis property tests that check any file passes the rules inferred from it
Found and fixed real bugs: Excel CSV files made the first column look missing, and a text bound crashed the check
CI with pinned actions, ruff security lint, and a job that tests the GitHub Action itself

projects.title: Honest Fit
projects.description: A local AI resume matcher that never invents skills you do not have.

caseStudy.problem: AI resume tools happily improve a resume by inventing skills and numbers. For a resume, that is the worst possible help.
built: A keyword analysis of about 170 skills that splits required from nice-to-have and quotes the resume line that proves each match
A local AI model through Ollama, so resumes never leave the computer and there is no API cost
An honesty guard that blocks any AI tip that adds a skill or a number the resume does not show
PDF and Word upload, parsed in a separate process with time and memory limits
results: About 99% line and branch test coverage, with Hypothesis property tests
Coverage-guided fuzzing with Atheris, which found a real PDF parsing bug that is now fixed
CodeQL, gitleaks, pip-audit, and a container scan on every push

projects.title: HelpDesk Autopilot
projects.description: Automates onboarding, offboarding, and password resets with approvals and an audit log.

caseStudy.problem: At small companies, one or two IT people handle every request by hand. Password resets eat the day, offboarding gets missed, and nobody can say who changed whose access or how long tickets take.
built: One-time password reset links that expire in 15 minutes
New-hire accounts and groups created from the request, and leavers disabled on their last day
Manager approval for access, plus a second IT approval for admin rights
An audit log the database itself refuses to delete
A web portal for employees, managers, and IT agents
Prometheus metrics and a Grafana SLA dashboard with alerts
results: A 90% test coverage gate and Playwright browser tests
CI with Trivy and CodeQL security scans
Portal security: directory sign-in, CSRF tokens, lockout after 5 wrong passwords, and a strict Content-Security-Policy

projects.title: Recipe Scaler

caseStudy.problem: Recipes are written for one number of people in one set of units, and they are hard to follow with messy hands.
built: Serving scaling that stays readable, like 1½ cups instead of 1.5
Scale to what you have, and switch between US and metric
Cook mode that keeps the screen on, with hands-free voice control
Import any pasted recipe, a pantry, and a shopping list that combines units
Works offline and installs like an app

recommendations.name: Adon Davis
recommendations.quote: He was comfortable taking on more complex functional testing than many of his peers and brought a level of patience and detail that was extremely valuable to the engineering team.
text: I had the opportunity to work closely with Abhirup Khan during his summer internship at SupplyBistro, where he served as a DevSecOps Intern and worked directly with me as CTO.

Abhirup contributed across build and release management, functional testing, test automation, database operations, AWS and GitHub secrets management, and DevSecOps documentation. He also helped move code through our development lifecycle from DEV to QA, staging, and ultimately production.

One of Abhirup’s strongest differentiators was his testing background. He was comfortable taking on more complex functional testing than many of his peers and brought a level of patience and detail that was extremely valuable to the engineering team. He also began work on automated testing and helped establish foundations that the team can continue to build on.

What I appreciated most about Abhirup was his persistence. When something was difficult or did not work immediately, he kept working the problem, sought help appropriately when needed, and focused on getting to a result.

He was also a dependable teammate. I frequently called on him to help newer DevSecOps interns, and he took initiative to document and even record knowledge-transfer sessions so others could continue the work effectively.
I would recommend Abhirup for junior DevSecOps, QA automation, release engineering, or related engineering roles where he can continue building on a solid technical foundation.

text: I taught Abhirup Khan in my graduate IT Project Management course at Illinois Institute of Technology, formerly known as IIT. Illinois Tech is recognized as being among the top 100 universities in the United States.

What struck me early on was that he wasn't approaching the material like a student trying to memorize facts to pass exams. He had already spent years as a QA Engineer working on enterprise systems and later moved into a DevSecOps role. As we discussed project risk, scope, and process improvement, he could immediately connect the concepts to situations he had experienced in the workplace. That kind of practical perspective is rare in a classroom, and it made his contributions valuable not only to his own learning but to the rest of the class as well.
He was always prepared and engaged. It did not surprise me to learn that he was later inducted into the Upsilon Pi Epsilon honor society. That is exactly the kind of student he was in my class.

Beyond his academic performance, Abhirup is easy to work with. He listens well, treats people with respect, and communicates clearly, qualities that are just as important in project management as technical ability.
I recommend Abhirup for any IT, DevSecOps, Quality Assurance, or IT leadership role. I am confident he would be an asset to any organization.

postmortems.title: Game day: full checkout outage in the Burn_Rate lab
postmortems.summary: A planned drill: every checkout request failed on purpose. The availability page fired 40 seconds after the first failure, the deploy gate blocked feature releases, a hotfix with a recorded reason got through, and the error rate was back under budget 311 seconds after the fix. The drill also showed how much a short history skews burn-rate alerts, and exposed a wrong assumption in my own tooling about when a page clears.

impact.label: Users affected
impact.value: None. This was the lab, on purpose

impact.label: Time to recover
impact.value: 311 seconds after the fix, measured by the 5 minute error rate

timeline.event: Deploy gate allows a release while checkout is healthy
Chaos switch on: every checkout fails
Deploy gate blocks feature releases: error budget exhausted
Hotfix allowed through the gate with a recorded reason
Recovered: 5 minute error rate back under the 0.5% budget

postmortems.rootCause: The outage itself was intentional. The findings were about the lab and my tooling. The lab had only minutes of history, so even the long alert windows (1 hour, 6 hours) held mostly outage data: the page fired after 40 seconds, and the slower 6x tier (6 hours and 30 minutes) fired too. That tier only clears once its 30 minute window recovers, but the first version of my game day script treated "page cleared" as proof of recovery, so it timed out even though the service was already healthy.
postmortems.detection: The fast-burn page fired in 40 seconds. That is faster than production would be: with days of history behind it, the same full outage pages after about 4.5 minutes, which the alert unit tests and the Lab on this site both show.
wentWell: The gate blocked features but still let the fix through, with the reason on record.
wentBadly: I treated "alert cleared" and "service recovered" as the same signal. They use different windows.
With minutes of history, the alerts and the 30 day budget (about -4,256%) were far more dramatic than they would be in production. Fine for a drill, misleading in a screenshot.

actions.action: Recovery is now judged by the 5 minute error rate dropping under budget; the page clears on its own later.
Alert unit tests and the Lab start with 3 days of healthy history, so their timings match production.
The Burn_Rate README explains why a page can outlive the incident.

postmortems.title: Load generator crash-looped in CI after a k6 2.x breaking change
postmortems.summary: The end-to-end CI run for Burn_Rate failed: Prometheus was scraping the checkout service but had recorded zero requests. The k6 load generator was crash-looping because k6 2.x removed the --no-summary flag I used. Fixed by switching to --summary-mode=disabled and making the rollout fail fast on startup crashes.

impact.label: What failed
impact.value: The Kubernetes CI workflow on main; no traffic meant no SLO data

impact.label: Time to fix
impact.value: Under an hour, the same evening

timeline.event: "Run the lab on kind" fails at "Prometheus is scraping checkout traffic": up=1 served=0
Pod list shows loadgen in CrashLoopBackOff with 5 restarts
Ran k6 2.3.0 locally with the same flags: --no-summary is no longer a flag
Fix: --summary-mode=disabled, checked against the real service (31 requests in 3 seconds)

postmortems.rootCause: The manifest pinned grafana/k6:2.3.0 but used a flag from k6 1.x, so the container exited at startup. The Deployment had no readiness check, so the rollout counted the pod as ready for a moment and the setup script reported success. The failure only surfaced later, as missing traffic.
postmortems.detection: The end-to-end CI job, which exists for exactly this. Unit tests and manifest validation had all passed.
wentWell: End-to-end CI caught a break that no unit test could.
The failure step printed pod status, which pointed straight at the crash loop.
wentBadly: The pinned image version and its flags were never run together before the push.
The rollout reported success for a container that was crashing.

actions.action: The load generator rollout waits 15 seconds (minReadySeconds), so a startup crash fails the setup script immediately.
The traffic check prints the load generator's logs when it fails.
Run the exact pinned version locally before changing its flags.

postmortems.title: Contact form sent messages, but visitors never saw the thank-you page
postmortems.summary: The new contact form emailed me every message, but after clicking Send the browser blocked the redirect back to the thank-you page, so the form looked stuck. Fixed the same day by allowing the site's own address in the Content-Security-Policy form-action rule.

impact.label: What failed
impact.value: The confirmation after sending: the page never changed and the fields kept their text

timeline.event: Contact form launched with Web3Forms and a strict Content-Security-Policy
My own test message arrived by email, but the thank-you page never loaded
Reproduced in a headless browser: Chrome blocked the redirect under form-action
Fix: form-action allows the site itself as well as api.web3forms.com
Verified in the browser, then shipped

postmortems.rootCause: form-action listed only https://api.web3forms.com. Web3Forms answers the form post with a redirect to abhirupkhan.me/thanks.html, and Chrome checks every hop of a form's redirect chain against form-action. The site's own address was not on the list, so the last hop was blocked.
postmortems.detection: I caught it in my own launch test. Unit tests checked the policy text, but nothing ran a real browser submission.
wentWell: Reproducing it in a headless browser made the cause obvious and proved the fix.
wentBadly: A strict policy was tested as text, not as behavior.
How form-action treats redirects is easy to miss.

actions.action: A test requires form-action to include the site itself whenever the form is on, with a comment explaining the redirect.
Test new forms with a real browser submission before launch.
